articles.text: Ballot item would renew City Parcel Tax for 12 years Piedmont City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore will provide an informational report on Measure F, a renewal of the Municipal Services Parcel Tax (City Services Tax) during a series of presentations at multiple city commission and committee meetings this month. Measure F, which will be on the March 5, 2024 ballot, would renew the City Services Tax for 12 years instead of the usual four and increase its tax rate by 20%- -an increase of between $12 and $21/month for most households. The City Council placed this renewal on the ballot at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. “The presentations before our citizen-led bodies will provide reliable and factual information on Measure F,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. “The City encourages everyone to participate in expressing what is important to them on Election Day. On March 5th, voters will be defining service level expectations for Piedmont.” The city’s decision to extend the term of the tax to 12 years is an attempt to increase the city’s ability for long-term planning. “This tax accounts for about 8 to 10% of general fund revenues,” said Echa Schneider, Communications Manager for the city. “Without knowing that money is going to be there, it makes it hard for the city to plan long term.” Schneider also added that the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committees have been encouraging the city to make this change for the past 15 years. The city briefly considered extending the term of the tax in 2019 but decided against it after the upheaval caused by the COVID-19 epidemic. The next presentation on Measure F will be on Thursday, January 25, at 5:30 p.m., at the Public Safety Committee meeting. All meetings will be held in City Council Chambers at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The Planning Commission meeting can also be viewed online or on KCOM-TV (Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T U-verse Channel 99). Measure F Presentation Schedule • Public Safety Committee: Thursday, January 25, 5:30 p.m. • Planning Commission: Monday, January 29, 5:30 p.m.

articles.text: Havens dad Jeff Hoffman won the 16th annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night tournament, on Friday, January 19, in the Veterans Hall with two pairs, queens over twos, to defeat Melissa Clark. During the four and half hour Texas-Hold-Em tournament, 148 other poker players were eliminated in a benefit that raised $52,000 for Havens Elementary School. Hosted by Dads Club President Roger Tsai, the event would not have been possible without 18 volunteers and many sponsors. The poker committee members included Francis Hoang, Andrew Johnson, Brandon Bercovich, Babak & Claudia Sanii, Jeff Nguyen, Reza Bazargani, Robert Dorsey, Kyle & Gretchen Killion, Matthew Waitkus, Susan Kagan, and Diana Lee. The tournament provided a fun environment with 150 players and around 70 more non-playing socializers. A beginners tutorial opened up the action to newbies and brought beginner’s luck fully into play. Gastronomy options included an ample snack table, Top-Dogs, Arthur Mac’s pizza, Chef Dorsey’s hors d’oeuvres, along with Oakland United Beerworks on tap. articles.text: Editor: I am a 40+ year resident of Piedmont. Because of Piedmont’s location relative to larger urban areas, there is increasing evidence of a need for enhanced city services, particularly for public safety. And of course, there is also the ongoing need to maintain and improve city property and utilities like parks, streets and storm drains. Quality city services like those we enjoy need to be paid for, and continuing this tax which we’ve regularly renewed for decades is how we need to pay for those services. For those reasons, I hope Piedmont’ Measure F succeeds in obtaining the necessary two-thirds vote for passage. –Michael Henn

articles.text: City of Piedmont ranks highest in county for clarity The nine Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the March 5, 2024 election, were evaluated in December 2023 and January 2024 by the Alameda County Chapter of the California Civil Grand Jury Association, (ACCGJA). The measures were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and The collective scores represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Civil Grand Jury Association members (up to 15 allowed). The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should be included in each type ACCGJA is not evaluating the merits of the measures. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot question put to the voters. State law requires ballot labels to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure, and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure”. Unfortunately, many jurisdictions violate the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one other than the agency promoting the measure is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a need for active and consistent monitoring and evaluation of local government’s ballot language. pages.text: Wednesday, January 24, 2024 3 The nine Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the March 5, 2024 election, were evaluated in December 2023 and January 2024 by the Alameda County Chapter of the California Civil Grand Jury Association, (ACCGJA). The measures were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and Other (non-tax measure). The collective scores represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Civil Grand Jury Association members (up to 15 allowed). The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should be included in each type of ballot measure. ACCGJA is not evaluating the merits of the measures. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot question put to the voters. State law requires ballot labels to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure, and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure”. Unfortunately, many jurisdictions violate the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one other than the agency promoting the measure is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a need for active and consistent monitoring and evaluation of local government’s ballot language. articles.text: The Year of the Dragon will be celebrated in Piedmont’s Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens Elementary School on Friday, February 9 from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) will host the annual Lunar New Year event highlighted by performances, crafts, a lion dance and dim sum. “It’s the Year of the Dragon, a year of energy and excitement. Last year’s event attracted many local Piedmont leaders and reached maximum enrollment prior to doors opening. Tickets are suggested to be reserved in advance by February 4 by emailing piedmontpaac@gmail.com or using the QR code. articles.text: State program to provide up to $3,000 for eligible households The City of Piedmont is encouraging residents to apply for the Earthquake Brace + Bolt retrofit program. Now through February 21, Piedmont homeowners may apply for a state retrofit grant and receive up to $3,000 to make their homes more resilient to earthquakes. Registration is only open for 30 days once per year. The Earthquake Brace + Bolt program is a state program that offers eligible homeowners grants of up to $3,000 to help offset the cost of seismic retrofits that would brace the walls of older homes and bolt houses to their foundations. These steps reduce the potential for damage or collapse in the event of an earthquake. Homes that qualify for the program are typically built before 1980 (but are more prevalent before 1940), have a raised continuous perimeter concrete foundation, may sit on level ground or a low slope, and may have woodframed walls (often called “cripple walls”) in the crawl space under the first floor. To apply for a retrofit grant, residents may visit www.earthquakebracebolt.com and complete the online registration form by February 21. The program

articles.text: The Troubadours will be busy in February as they celebrate Valentine’s Day on February 14 with Heart-O-Grams in collaboration with ASB. On Valentine’s Day, members of the Troubadours will accompany students from ASB as they go from classroom to classroom delivering paper telegrams and spreading holiday cheer with their harmonious voices. The Troubadours are a wellknown, completely student-run a capella group that’s been serenading Piedmont since 1968. Between their infectious energy and melodic voices, the Troubadours have a long-standing reputation at the high school for being creative, performance-oriented, and fun. “It’s just kids who are passionate about music and have a common goal of learning music together and spreading joy and performing for others as well,” said senior Cat Pasion. There are three directors, two program directors, and a musical director, all of whom are seniors elected by other members. The directors run rehearsals, schedule gigs, organize bonding events and retreats, teach, arrange and select music, and hold auditions. “I had never been in a fully student-run organization but I think it really teaches our leaders how to become responsible and be able to learn the skills we need for future jobs,” said junior Lauren Brenner. Brenner has been a part of the Troubadours since her freshman year. The Troubadours just finished a busy winter season, as many organizations look for holiday carolers for events. The Troubs perform routinely during December at Scott’s Restaurant in Jack London Square, at private gatherings, and at local events, including the annual Piedmont Tree Lighting ceremony. Last month, the group made their annual delivery of Holiday-O-Grams amidst the stressful weeks of preparations for final exams. The Holiday-O-Grams are a short break during class that helps put everyone in the holiday spirit. The week prior to deliveries, students can buy small notes for friends that members of ASB deliver to each classroom as the Troubs, in their festive costumes, sing to their peers. “It was so much fun. I just loved dressing up and bombarding all the classrooms with songs,” said freshman Ben Ramakrishnan. “It’s the highlight of my day,” said junior Kaeli Yeung. “It brightens up the school atmosphere, “ said junior Teresa McKay. Holiday-O-Grams were not only a highlight for students, but for teachers as well. “I can’t stop smiling every time they walk into the room because it’s just so joyful,” said History teacher and Yearbook Adviser Melanie McCauley. “I love that the Troubs are so comfortable coming in and singing in front of everyone. I love it when I see students, ones I had no idea could sing, all of a sudden come in and start belting out songs. I hope it never goes away.” The Troubadours will also hold a Spring Concert in May. The Troubadours are available for hire for private events. For more information, contact program directors Axel Saldanha or Melina Markowitz at thepiedmonttroubadours@gmail.com The Troubadours, Piedmont High School’s a cappella vocal ensemble, shown during their busy holiday season in December.

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation’s (PEF) Giving Campaign resulted in donations of $3.4 million from 1,160 households in support of Piedmont schools. The number of donors, and the total amount donated, increased from last year. According to PEF Board Chair Tonya Antonucci, “This increase is a tremendous accomplishment. PUSD enrollment has declined, but we’re seeing both a higher rate of community participation and an increase in the dollar amounts donated.” Antonucci credits the leadership of Co-Chairs Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn for the campaign’s success. The PEF board and Giving Campaign committee, the PUSD School Board, and the boards of Havens and PMS parents clubs all achieved 100% parent participation in the campaign. Overall 66% of PUSD parents made a contribution this year compared with 62% last year. Winning the class level competition was transitional kindergarten (TK) with 83% parent participation. Of the six schools, Havens came out ahead with 82% participation with Havens’ Kindergarten parents leading at 92% participation. A party to celebrate TK families is being planned for early spring. Co-Chair Kim Hunter said, “We thank everyone who contributed. This has been a lot of work and a lot of fun, and seeing the community come together for something this important is so rewarding.” Catie Osborn added, “It has made me realize how important each individual is when making sure our schools succeed. And how much more we have to do. There’s a lot of work still to be done at the national, state and local levels.” “That’s why we’re both stepping up again to chair next year’s Giving Campaign,” said Hunter. “We know we can count on everyone to help us out again.” Funds raised through the Giving Campaign will be granted to PUSD for use during the 2024- 25 school year. For more information on the grant process and this year’s grant distribution, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/ Our-Impact.

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting tonight Wednesday, January 24 at 7:00 p.m. at City Hall. The meeting is shaping up for high drama as the teachers union has ramped up its visibility in town with picketing, and two days of coordinated “work to rule” action. The teachers union will reveal the results of their Strike Authorization Vote at tonight’s board meeting. The five school board members, led by President Veronica Anderson Thigpen will be joined by Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Teachers Union President Elise Marks will give the result of the Strike Authorization Vote to the board and the community during the Board President’s announcement. Outside of the ongoing impasse over teacher salary negotiations, the meeting will have several topics of wide interest. An announcement will be made that the application period for the annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award has opened, and that the school district will recognize February as Black History Month. A summary of the Governor’s Proposed State Budget for 2024-25 and its potential impact on Piedmont School District will be provided by Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The update is coming on the heels of the January 10 release of Governor Gavin Newsom’s Proposed State budget. The results of a financial audit of the district will also be presented as a review and action item. The agenda for the board meeting can be found at Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/SB_Meetings/ViewMeeting.aspx- ?S=36030373&MID=27600 The board meeting can be attended in person at City Hall, or participated in remotely via Zoom.us/j/82270330787

articles.text: Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret the weekend of February 1-4 at the Alan Harvey Theater. Directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead, this Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close, explores the exhilarating life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms have been omitted. Memorable songs from Cabaret include “Willkommen,” “Perfectly Marvelous”, “Money”, “Maybe This Time”, and the title song , “Cabaret”. More than 70 Piedmont and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Schultz,” said sophTheo Ferguson (left) (Cliff Bradshaw), Amelia Addington (Sally Bowles), Caitlin Boothby (Emcee), Ellie Broscow (Fräulein Schneider), and Ben Wakefield (Herr Schultz) omore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Senior Ellie Broscow, who plays the role of Fräulein Schneider, added, “Cabaret is an incredibly important musical to me and has been for quite some time. My love for the show has definitely grown throughout the rehearsal process as I’ve realized just how relevant the themes still are, 58 years since its premiere on Broadway in 1996. The themes of anti-Semitism especially resonate with me after the events of October 7th. I have seen how the world has turned against the Jewish people throughout history, and Cabaret addresses a particularly intense period, 1929, or the rise of Hitler. The vivid anti-Semitism that existed then has continued to increase, especially right now, and we simply cannot turn a blind eye to it any longer. I hope that Cabaret will continue to be performed for years to come.” Performances are February 1, 2, 3, and 4 at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket. articles.text: Highlander Robotics Team 8033’s SPARK fundraiser will be held on Friday, January 26 at 7 p.m. at a lovely central Piedmont home. Enjoy a talk by a local tech luminary that is sure to spark conversation while you enjoy delicious wine and food. This event directly supports Piedmont’s Highlander Robotics Team 8033, a program designed to empower youths to be leaders in STEM. Tickets are now on sale through our website www. frc8033.com The event features Bryan Cantrill’s talk Intelligence Is Not Enough about AI and ethics, a timely topic for parents of kids interested in STEM. Cantrill is a software engineer who has spent over a quarter of a century at the hardware/software interface. He is the co-founder and CTO of Oxide Computer Company, the creator of the world’s first commercial cloud computer. Formerly CTO of Joyent and Distinguished Engineer of Sun Microsystems, Cantrill is a sought-after speaker in the tech industry for his ability to colorfully connect strong values to current best practices. As the Scoutmaster of Piedmont’s Troop 1, he is also committed to leadership formation of our youth. History of team Highlander Robotics Team 8033 was founded in 2019 to provide access to engineering through competitive robotics for high school students of Piedmont and nearby Bay Area communities. Our student-led approach is designed to empower our youth to become leaders in the growth of STEM education while advocating for gender parity in tech. We are role models in our community by embracing a culture of excellence and innovation in a fun and collaborative environment. Team 8033 is the capstone robotics program for the largest community-based FIRST league in the country, organized by Piedmont Makers. We partner with Piedmont School DisBryan Cantrill is the featured speaker at a fundraiser on January 26 for Highlander Robotics. trict to have our homebase in the Mary G. Ross engineering lab at Piedmont High School. We are the only competitive community-based FRC team in a 25-mile radius and now have team members from 15 high schools who otherwise would not be able to participate in FRC. Beyond access to the robust network of Bay Area FIRST FRC teams, we provide hands-on experience with our lab equipment and technology; engagement with expert mentors and speakers from STEM companies; and opportunities for field trips to top companies. Because it is a community-based team, it does not receive funding from schools. The team’s goal is to cover half of its $80,000 annual budget from contributions from the community and from corporate donations. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Staff photo – Pouyan Assadi Head track & field coach, Piedmont High School Witter Field is expected to open on February 5, two months later than expected. The track will be out of service until later this summer, effectively displacing the track and field team with 104 athletes. Construction on the renovation of Witter Field hasn’t gone as planned in the slightest. After having an initial target date of November 2023, the field’s completion has been pushed back continuously, leaving fall and winter sports teams forced out of town for home games. According to Piedmont High athletic director Bradley Smet, some sports can return to Witter Field starting February 5, but with strings attached. One bright note is Smet’s assurance that the girls’ and boys’ lacrosse teams will have a full spring season at Witter Field. “Right now, we have work that’s happening on February 1. They are re-laying asphalt that needed work after a section of the field degraded that they did not anticipate. That led to additional work. As long as weather cooperates, we’ll be able to get back on the field by February 5,” Smet said. But Smet explained that repairs to the track won’t start until June and won’t be completed for one month. It means that the track and field team of 10 athletes will not have a training or competition site for its upcoming season. “They are doing the work on the track over summer. My understanding is that Witter Field would be shut down, once again, in June in order to lay the track surface,” said Smet. “As long as there are no more delays, we’re looking at opening things back up again in July,” Smet said. The track and field team has been forced to find a training site off campus with completion of the track not expected until late summer. They’ll be splitting time at Laney College and Witter Field’s turf field going forward. “We’re going to use a combination of Witter Field and Laney, which will be the home-base. We’re going to try and mix in Witter,” said head track and field coach Pouyan Assadi. “We’re envisioning that we’ll have the field available for short sprint workouts. Soccer and lacrosse will be prioritized, but we’ve talked to those coaches and they are very understanding of the situation. We’re all working through this together.” “The asphalt-track will be available, but I envision us doing short sprint workouts on Witter Field itself. We’ll use Laney for hurdles, jumps and pole vaults, and we’ll use the Witter weight room and the hills in the neighborhood as well,” Complications at Witter Field have strongly impacted the school’s running programs going back to the fall. Without a track to train on, Assadi has been forced to host practices at local parks. He stressed the importance of how an adequate running surface plays a factor in student-athletes’ health and well-being, in addition. tain Xander Schulte-Sasse’s season was cut short last fall. He’s eying a return to distance events in track this spring bit without a home field track. Longtime resident and distance running coach Steve Zirkelbach said, “It’s been hard on the kids. We’re doing the best we can with the hand we have been dealt. As a coach of young runners, one of my biggest concerns has been the increased risk of injuries from exclusively running on hard surfaces. Not having the track’s softer running surface significantly increases risk of injury. I believe some of the injuries we sustained last fall may have been avoided if we trained on a more forgiving surface. It’s a bummer that hundreds of Piedmont kids have been displaced.” “There seems to be something unpredictable every four weeks. We get the disappointing news along with the rest of the public. I’m a coach, I’m also a dad, and I pay taxes in town. Not just in property tax, but the extra money I spent to have a house here is because of the great public schools which presumably has excellent decision-makers. “It sure would be nice to know some details; my intention is to be here 20-plus years,” Assadi said. A November completion would’ve allowed the football team to finish its season on a home field. The squad won the 2023 WACC Shoreline Title and a berth in the post-season North Coast Section playoffs all while training on a portion of the outfield of the baseball field. Both soccer teams are coming off 2023 NCS title-winning seasons, but they have been forced split their home games at Chabot College in Hayward and Estuary Park in Alameda. Both teams hosted practices at Laney College this season. A February 5 start date would allow Piedmont’s boys’ and girls soccer teams to play their first home games at Witter Field in 62 days – since the season started two months ago on December 5. The girls’ soccer team’s critical home match with rival Bishop O’Dowd on February 6 is its next to last game of the regular season. “Coaches have been asked to be very creative. The problem is with the rain coming down, all the plyometric and sprint workouts we want to do on softer surfaces to protect the kids’ knees, ankles, feet and joints are being done in Piedmont Park, which isn’t flat anywhere. “Also, the Rec. Department has asked us to use a smaller space so we don’t take up too much space for the regular patrons. We found another patch of grass, but its muddy and the kids are going home dirty. We’re probably able to do 25-40 percent of what we’d normally do. “The coaches have been creative. We’ll still be able to accomplish quite a bit this season,” Assadi said. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team reeled in three more wins last week to extend its winning streak to five games. They defeated San Leandro 61-50 at home on Wednesday, January 17, beat Castro Valley 56-42 on Friday, January 19 at the Trojans’ home court, and traveled to Kentfield the following day for a 56-44 victory over Marin Catholic. (Final stats against Castro Valley were not provided.) The five-game winning streak has coincided with the return of senior forward Declan Linnane. The two-sport (also water polo) provides stability in the low post, defense, and is a player who can knock down a 3-pointer in the corner in critical moments. “It’s great to have Declan back. He’s like a shutdown cornerback on the left side. This 3-2 zone that we have has given a bit of an identity defensively. With his water polo background, he deflects four or five passes a game because he’s so long,” said coach Ben Spencer of the senior. “I’m just happy to be back,” said Linnane. “It was tough sitting out and watching the team battle, but other guys got a lot of minutes and that was good for them.”. A big part of this year’s team is sophomore guard Dillon Casey, emerging as a starter following senior forward Alex Anderson’s injury in the first game of the season. “I’m definitely learning from the upperclassmen and taking in all I can from them. It’s been an easy transition; my teammates have made it really easy. As a point guard, protecting the ball is one of the most important parts of the game, so that’s something I’m working on,” said Casey The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 12-7 overall and 4-2 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team suffered two narrow losses to Western Alameda County Conference opponents last week, falling 1-0 to rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, January 18, and taking a 2-1 loss to Encinal on Tuesday, January 16. The pair of losses extends the Highlanders’ winless run to four matches and still seeking their first league victory. PHS dominated possession against Encinal but couldn’t find the finishing touch. The Highlanders came close to scoring on multiple occasions against O’Dowd as well, but the Dragons were able to sit defensively after taking a 1-0 lead in the ninth minute. “I felt we’re playing well; we just need to figure out how to solve the problems to break down the other teams. We couldn’t do it against Encinal and couldn’t do it tonight [against O’Dowd]. But you hear the girls. They are happy and enjoying it; they know they are putting forward a good team effort. We’ll keep plugging away,” said coach Dan Chubbock Staff Photos Freshman Elsa Wallway was shoved down in the box against Bishop O’Dowd, but there was no penalty call. Amy Derr sends in a long ball in the final moments against O’Dowd. Piedmont looks to regroup after a pair of narrow league losses. following the result to O’Dowd. 1-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont nearly struck first in the fourth minute of the game when Miranda Liu tracked a long pass into the penalty area. But the Dragons’ keeper came far out of net to get a hand on Liu’s shot. The ball skipped back towards the net but a BOD defender raced back to clear it off the line. Three minutes later O’Dowd struck after playing a long ball into space to their speedy striker, who caught Piedmont’s defense in a vulnerable spot and slotted in her shot in a one-on-one situation. From there, the Dragons sat deeper, having their keeper far up the penalty box waiting to pounce on forward passes to Liu. After a couple of shot attempts, Wallway was involved in a controversial no-call in the 35th minute. She dribbled into the box with two defenders chasing her and fell to the ground after taking a shove in the back. The referee waived his arms to signal no foul. In the second half, Wallway had a shot through traffic in the 55th minute, and PHS drew corner kicks in the 66th and 75th. A ball was played short to Wallway and tried to bend in a shot from the top of the box, but it went narrowly wide of the far post. Piedmont had one final free kick in second half stoppage time, when Amy Derr sent in a long ball from midfield. The pass fell into a dangerous area, but the Highlanders didn’t put contact on the ball and the Dragons’ keeper made the claim. 2-1 loss to Encinal On a cold and stormy night at Chabot College in Hayward, Piedmont couldn’t find the finishing touch past Encinal’s keeper. Lola Beihn had a shot on target in the early going, but the Jets’ GK was in good position. Encinal scored in the first half after a ball trickled around without clearance, it fortunately fell to an attack to send in a low shot for the score. As the rain continued, massive puddles on the field began slowing down every pass, leading to difficulties in Piedmont’s quick-moving and fluid style. Liu had a near chance midway through the first after beating two defenders to put herself one-onone with the goalie, but her leftfooted shot clanged off the crossbar. Liu had another shot hit off the crossbar minutes later. Wallway tied the match in the second half, using her speed to pounce on a loose ball around midfield and wheel her way into a one-on-one situation. She took a touch as the Encinal keeper rushed out, sending in a shot to the empty net. Wallway had another shot on target moments later. PHS continued pressing forward for a goal with multiple shots being saved or going narrowly wide. But disaster struck in last minute of the game when Encinal had one of its only attacks in the second half, where their forward sent in a beautiful arcing shot from the top of the box.

Two of Piedmont High School’s former basketball stars are having impressive collegiate seasons. Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020 and now a redshirt junior at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, is in the midst of a career year. He was recently named West Coast Conference Player of the Week after leading his team to a 66-46 win over Kent State on December 29. During the game, he scored a career-high of 19 points, converting seven of nine shots from the field, including two 3-pointers. He also grabbed six rebounds including three offensive boards, to go along with one blocked shot. Since then, Barrett scored 14 points and had seven rebounds in an 81-70 win over UC San Diego, and he scored 17 points and had six rebounds in a 74-49 win over Santa Clara. The Gaels are now 13-6 and 4-0 in conference play, in first place in the WACC. Barrett has appeared in all 19 games thus far, averaging 16.1 minutes per game, totaling 94 points with 33 field goals and 10 three-pointers, to go along with 10 assists and 10 steals. He’s been active on the boards with 64 rebounds, including 34 offensive grabs. St. Mary’s finished last season ranked No. 22 in the country after going 27-8. They received the No. 5 seed in the NCAA Tournament, defeating No. 12 VCU 63-51 in the first round before losing 70-55 to UConn. As a sophomore, Barrett made an appearance in the Gaels’ 82- 53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament. While at Piedmont High he helped lead the school to the North Coast Section Div. 4 championship. He was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in his senior year. As a sophomore, Harris helped lift Carleton College to the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference championship with an 86-76 win over St. Johns on February 26, where the guard scored 19 points. Harris was second on the team in scoring with 16.4 points per game achieved double-digit points in 20 of 24 games last season, including eight games with at least 20 points. He led Carleton with 92 assists, was second on the team in field goals with 159 made, and was third in rebounds with 132. Carleton finished last year with a 24-4 overall record before losing 81-77 to St. Norbert in the first round of the Division 3 NCAA tournament. He graduated from Piedmont High as another all-time great, finishing with over 1,200 career points as a three-year starter in three highly successful years: 21-11 in his sophomore year, winner of the North Coast Section championship in 2020 with a 24-6 record, and 11-5 in the pandemic shortened 2021 season. Harris was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in 2021. LUKE HARRIS Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota and recently surpassed 1,000 collegiate points after scoring 23 against Macalester on January 10. The Knights are currently 9-6. Harris has appeared in all 15 games and is averaging 31.9 minutes per game. He’s recorded 324 points with 103 field goals and 13 three-pointers, converting 44.6 percent of his field goals to go along with 51 assists and 31 steals. Luke Harris, Class of 2021, recently surpassed 1,000 collegiate points with Carleton College. He was Piedmont Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021.

articles.text: Principal ballerina leaves an unprecedented and high-profile role in the world of dance San Francisco Ballet Principal Dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance with San Francisco Ballet on Wednesday, February 14, at 7:30 p.m., dancing the role of Marguerite in Sir Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand at the War Memorial Opera House. Tan will also dance with former SF Ballet Principal Dancer Tiit Helimets in a selection from Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight at the company’s 2024 Opening Night Gala on Wednesday, January 24, 2024. The veteran dancer made headlines earlier this month when she announced her departure from the company after a record-breaking 29 seasons. Tan joined SF Ballet in 1995 as a soloist. In a meteoric rise through the ranks, she advanced to the coveted role of Principal Dancer within two years, making her the youngest principal dancer in the company’s history at age 20. Now 47, she is the longest-dancing principal with SF Ballet to date. Over her long and memorable career, Tan has danced in nearly 100 classical, neoclassical, and contemporary ballets choreographed by the likes of George Balanchine, Sir Kenneth MacMillan, John Neumeier, Christopher Wheeldon, Helgi Tomasson, Yuri Possokhov, Edwaard Liang, and Wayne McGregor, among others. In a recent statement, Tan took a moment to thank her fans for their support over the years. “Finally, to the San Francisco audiences over the last three decades, I express my sincere thanks. Your belief in me has been a driving force, and I am grateful for the inspiration you have provided,” said Tan. After her tenure with the company, Tan has stated that she intends to continue dancing and giving performances, albeit in other settings. Tickets to Yuan Yuan Tan’s farewell performance on February 14 may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling (415) 865-2000, Monday to Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Photo by Erik Tomasson Yuan Yuan Tan in a performance of Liang’s the Infinite Ocean in 2020

articles.text: Cal Performances at UC Berkeley presents a special Bay Area premiere of The Rite of Spring by choreographer Pina Bausch, in addition to common ground[s] by Germaine Acogny and Malou Airaudo at Zellerbach Hall the weekend of Friday-Sunday, February 16-18. Bausch’s seminal and towering The Rite of Spring (1975) — staged in the Bay Area for the first time ever — is performed by an ensemble of over 30 dancers from 14 African countries, assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells theater. The work’s companion piece, common ground[s], is a new duet co-created and danced by septuagenarians Germaine Acogny, known as the “mother of African contemporary dance,” and Malou Airaudo, a longtime collaborator with Bausch. The duet contemplates the performers’ lived experiences, their relationship to dance across generations, and their identities as mothers, daughters, grandmothers and granddaughters. “This is the first time that The Rite of Spring is done not with an existing company, but with dancers who came together specifically for this piece,” said Salomon Bausch, Pina Bausch’s son and Executive Director of the Pina Bausch Foundation. “I’m very excited to see the impact of their personalities and their diverse dance backgrounds on the piece but also vice versa — how the piece influences the dancers, both as artists and as human beings.” Tickets ($33-$96) for the show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@ calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) celebrates its 87th season with the 2024 Winter Concert this Saturday, January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church, 7:30 p.m. This year marks Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 34th season as YPSO’s Music Director and Conductor and features an inaugural collaboration with a longstanding Bay Area institution, the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO). The two groups will feature BCCO classical soprano singer Vuyiswa Sigadi and solo violinist Henry Stroud, the YPSO concertmaster. A sophomore at Berkeley High School, he is the winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. The concert opens with American composer Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum, a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination. YPSO will then perform the first movement of Camille SaintSaëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61. According to the program notes of Orrin Howard, the violin concerto’s “first movement revolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” Closing the program is Francis Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. Poulenc’s Gloria is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures which will be led by BCCO Music Director Ming Luke, Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. articles.text: The first retrospective of artist Pacita Abad, on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, will have its last day this Sunday, January 28. Featuring over 40 major works, including many rarely seen by the public, this exhibition is the most significant U.S. presentation of the artist’s multifaceted and mesmerizing art practice. Throughout her 32-year career from the 1970s to the early 2000s, If My Friends Could See Me Now (1991), one of the many trapunto paintings by the artist Pacita Abad at SFMOMA. The exhibit closes this Sunday, January 28. Abad centered the triumphs and adversities of people on the periphery of power, as seen in her Social Realist, Immigrant Experience and Masks and Spirits series. This exhibition celebrates an artist whose vibrant and inventive practice generated thousands of daring artworks—from intricately constructed underwater scenes to abstract compositions—and whose themes are as urgent today as they were two decades ago. Abad was born on 1946 in Basco, Philippines; and died 2004 in Singapore. She traveled and lived in over 60 countries in her lifetime including Bangladesh, Papua New Guinea, the Dominican Republic, Kenya, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Sudan and Yemen. San Francisco in particular was a place of creativity for Abad, as the city inspired her artistic career in the early 1970s. Abad interacted with myriad communities through her travels, incorporating a diversity of artistic traditions and techniques – from Korean ink brush painting to Indonesian batik and Nigerian tie-dye – into her expansive practice. These lessons found their greatest expression in her trapunto paintings: canvases that she painted, stuffed and embellished with buttons, cowrie shells, beads and mirrors. She created hundreds of these magnificently textured works, occasionally enlisting the help of family members and friends, thereby evoking the communal cultures that inspired her. “When curator Nancy Lim and I learned that this exhibition was being planned, we knew that it had to come to San Francisco, the city that inspired Pacita Abad to commit her life to artistic expression,” said Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at SFMOMA. “While some of the works gathered here were shown locally during Abad’s lifetime, this is the first exhibition to reveal the profundity of her prolific practice.” SFMOMA is open from 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday (closed Wednesday), and 1 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 for adults, $25 ages 65+, $23 ages 19-24, free 18 and younger, free for members) are available online at sfmoma.org, or in-person at the museum counter.
articles.title: Pacita Abad art exhibit closes this Sunday at SFMOMA

articles.text: Sound Sculpture by MASARY Studios, featured at Glow: Discover the art of light, on view at the SF Exploratorium through this Sunday, Jan. 28. The San Francisco Exploratorium’s annual celebration of luminous artworks, Glow: Discover the art of light, will run through this Sunday, January 28. Visitors can compose music with light, play LED-lit dungeon crawl games, and see themselves in mechanical mirrors through the work of seven artists. Among the large-scale light and sound installations are Sound Sculpture by MASARY Studios and Flux by Collectif Scale. Build dynamic musical compositions by moving Sound Sculpture’s portable location-aware cubes around, changing the rhythm and pitch as the cubes shift. Meanwhile, the Exploratorium presents the U.S. premiere of Flux, which showcases 48 twirling rods of white light that appear to twist and coil – put on a headset to immerse yourself in synchronized compositions by Grégory Sémah. Experience interactive artworks by Robin Baumgartner, including Quantum Jungle, a mathematically accurate model of a quantum object, and Line Wobbler, a challenging LED dungeon crawl game where hand-eye coordination is key. Crystal Paintings by Maria Constanza Ferreira reveals the hidden, brilliant patterns found in crystals, and you can also view a selection of Ferreira’s short films in the Osher Gallery 1 Microcinema. Chaco Kato’s Color Study makes its U.S. premiere at the show, featuring constantly changing colors and geometric patterns projected onto a solid but seemingly weightless artwork made of thousands of pieces of string. Her journey unfolds as a passionate photographer who finds solace and inspiration in the quiet moments of life. Pacita Abad art exhibit closes this Sunday at SFMOMA Abad centered the triumphs and adversities of people on the periphery of power, as seen in her Social Realist, Immigrant Experience and Masks and Spirits series. This exhibition celebrates an artist whose vibrant and inventive practice generated thousands of daring artworks—from intricately constructed underwater scenes to abstract compositions—and whose themes are as urgent today as they were two decades ago. Abad was born on 1946 in Basco, Philippines; and died 2004 in Singapore. She traveled and lived in over 60 countries in her lifetime including Bangladesh, Papua New Guinea, the Dominican Republic, Kenya, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Sudan and Yemen. San Francisco in particular was a place of creativity for Abad, as the city inspired her artistic career in the early 1970s. Abad interacted with myriad communities through her travels, incorporating a diversity of artistic traditions and techniques – from Korean ink brush painting to Indonesian batik and Nigerian tie-dye – into her expansive practice. These lessons found their greatest expression in her trapunto paintings: canvases that she painted, stuffed and embellished with buttons, cowrie shells, beads and mirrors. As everyone probably knows, both Mozart and BeethoThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet ven suffered from a variety of psychological illnesses. Mozart was one of the first people who was noted to have Tourette’s syndrome. He would frequently blurt out scatological comments. This mercurial personality is readily observed in his music. He’ll state an idea and then do about face. Everything is always kept in perfect symmetry, however. I’d like to mention the French composer-pianist St-Saens at this time. We are fortunate that he made a number of recordings and a silent film. Riveting. And filled with one grand chase scene after the next. Often they were serials that defined the word cliffhanger. articles.text: Lat week’s Walking on Wednesday group included Bill Ahern, Irene Thompson, Quincy and Helen Dong, Joanne Larson, Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Melba Yee, Swee Ling Chen, Kat Lang, Helene Farber, Chuck Oraftik, Lori Austin, Nancy Henn, Tina Shum, Rick Eigenbrode, Stella Houston, Sharona Fischrup, Martin Levy, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Mike Henn, Peggy Shultz, Maricela Negron, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Matt Gerhardt, Nancy and Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Elizabeth Richter, Phil Witte, Ken Hubbert, Pat Keller, Adrienne Hamlin, Edith Lee, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Joyce Ahern, Claudine Bach, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kuo, Noemi Alvarado and Mark Davis, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 47 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday, January 17. There is some impressive Piedmont City and School District construction going on around town. Two new “bulb-outs,” also called “curb extensions,” are being built at the intersections of Oakland and El Cerrito Avenues and Oakland and Jerome Avenues. At Nova and Magnolia Avenues, a new traffic island is in the works, too. Steel beams have been erected for the new building at the Piedmont Community Pool site. Additionally, Witter Field and its track are getting new surfaces. The walkers thought it would be interesting to check out all of them, so a loop to all five was selected as the morning’s route. The group went down Magnolia Avenue to look at the progress on the pool. They were able to see a lot more than on past visits. The construction fence that surrounds the project had been pulled back in places. The shape of the facility with its building and two pools could be better envisioned now that the steel beams are up, and at the back is a massive, new, concrete retaining wall. The project was approved by voters in November 2020, and $19.5 million worth of bonds were authorized at that time when interest rates were low. The new facility replaces the original mid- 20th Century Piedmont Pool that was leaking water each day and no longer met the community’s needs. Designs for the new aquatics center were developed with extensive community input. However, the building’s size had to be reduced and other modifications made in May 2022 when construction bids came in higher than expected. Incremental funding was obtained to make the facility a unique all-electric design. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation led fundraising for landscaping. Construction started on January 27, 2023 with expectations that pool should open later this year. The group then went down Magnolia to the foot of El Cerrito Avenue to see the Witter resurfacing project. The new artificial turf looked good, but it appeared work needed to be done on the track. It was reported that cracks in large portions of the track’s surface had been discovered. Additional work and $155,500 more from Piedmont School District are needed to complete this approximately $4.9 million project to be funded by a State facilities grant. It was started in June 2023, but the expected February completion day is in question now. After Witter Field, they headed to Magnolia to Nova to see the first of the City’s street projects, a new traffic island. The site’s old bollards will be removed and curbing work has started. Then, it was up Nova to Jerome and Oakland Avenue to see the first of the bulb-outs. City Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said these curb extensions will make the areas safer by increasing pedestrian visibility, shortening road-crossing distances, and reducing vehicle speeds by narrowing the streets. Construction began on January 8 and is expected to be completed in three to four months. Traffic control by a construction flagman was helpful in getting the parade-like column of walkers across Oakland Avenue. Next it was up Oakland to see the bulb-out at El Cerrito Avenue. There was a significant carve out of the sidewalk, but no work was being done on it at the time. The total construction cost for the three locations is $773,885. Funding comes from a $50,000 Piedmont Beautification Foundation contribution and approximately $600,000 from the State Gas Tax. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Nestled in the heart of France, the Rhone Valley is a historic wine region extending from Lyon in the north to the Camargue area near the Mediterranean Sea in the south. Enriched by the Rhone River, which originates in the Swiss Alps and meanders through its valleys, the Rhone region has over 2,000 years of viticulture history dating back to the ancient Greeks. This picturesque landscape not only holds a profound historical and cultural significance but also serves as the nurturing ground for a diverse range of grape varieties, giving birth to some of the world’s most esteemed wines. The first cultivated vines in the Rhône valley were possibly planted around 600 BC. Syrah and Viognier are speculated to be the two most prominent grape varieties in the Northern Rhône. Some believe that Greeks brought Syrah grapes from the Persian city of Shiraz. Others say that the grape came from the Sicilian city of Syracuse, from whence the Romans sailed up the Rhône valley with Syrah and Viognier grapes. After the collapse of the Roman Empire, Popes gave fresh impetus to a flourishing wine trade in the region. In 1737, the King announced that all casks for resale should have the brand name C.D.R. (Côtes du Rhône). Just over 100 years later, wines from other parts of the region were added to the C.D.R. definition. Usually, Rhône reds are produced with Syrah and Grenache. Other red Rhône varietals are Mourvedre, Counoise, and Cinsault. Expect a fruity flavor and aroma that you’ll never forget. Indeed, Rhône whites feature a variety of flavors according to the dominant grape. The most common white Rhône varietals are Roussanne, Marsanne, Grenache Blanc, Viognier, and Clairette Blanche. The northern region of Rhône has a cooler climate because of the mistral wind that blows through the area. This region accounts for a very small percentage of total Rhône wine production. However, the Northern Rhône produces the most exclusive wines. Syrah is the only allowed grape variety here, but most of the AOCs allow a small amount of Marsanne or Roussanne in the blend. Cornas AOC is the exception, where any red wine must be 100% Syrah. The Southern Rhône wine region benefits from a modern Mediterranean climate. It has warmer summers and milder winters. The south region boasts an amazing variety of grapes. Two categories of wine are ‘Left’ and ‘Right’, which actually refer to the banks of the Rhône River. The left category features bigger wines with fuller and fruitier flavors. The Southern boasts a wealth of appellations that stretch from either side of the river into the mountains and valleys. The following wines represent some of the wonderful Rhone wines that are available on the market today. The Rhone wines also provide a good bargain. With the prices of Bordeaux and Burgundy wine skyrocketing, it is nice to find that all the wines reviewed here are less than $30.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 24, 2024 23 The Wine Corner Rhone Valley Wines By Pierre DuMont Nestled in the heart of France, the Rhone Valley is a historic wine region extending from Lyon in the north to the Camargue area near the Mediterranean Sea in the south. Enriched by the Rhone River, which originates in the Swiss Alps and meanders through its valleys, the Rhone region has over 2,000 years of viticulture history dating back to the ancient Greeks. This picturesque landscape not only holds a profound historical and cultural significance but also serves as the nurturing ground for a diverse range of grape varieties, giving birth to some of the world’s most esteemed wines. The first cultivated vines in the Rhône valley were possibly planted around 600 BC. Syrah and Viognier are speculated to be the two most prominent grape varieties in the Northern Rhône. Some believe that Greeks brought Syrah grapes from the Persian city of Shiraz. Others say that the grape came from the Sicilian city of Syracuse, from whence the Romans sailed up the Rhône valley with Syrah and Viognier grapes. After the collapse of the Roman Empire, Popes gave fresh impetus to a flourishing wine trade in the region. In 1737, the King announced that all casks for resale should have the brand name C.D.R. (Côtes du Rhône). Just over 100 years later, wines from other parts of the region were added to the C.D.R. definition. Usually, Rhône reds are produced with Syrah and Grenache. Other red Rhône varietals are Mourvedre, Counoise, and Cinsault. Expect a fruity flavor and aroma that you’ll never forget. Indeed, Rhône whites feature a variety of flavors according to the dominant grape. The most common white Rhône varietals are Roussanne, Marsanne, Grenache Blanc, Viognier, and Clairette Blanche. The northern region of Rhône has a cooler climate because of the mistral wind that blows through the area. This region accounts for a very small percentage of total Rhône wine production. However, the Northern Rhône produces the most exclusive wines. Syrah is the only allowed grape variety here, but most of the AOCs allow a small amount of Marsanne or Roussanne in the blend. Cornas AOC is the exception, where any red wine must be 100% Syrah. The Southern Rhône wine region benefits from a modern Mediterranean climate. It has warmer summers and milder winters. The south region boasts an amazing variety of grapes. Two categories of wine are ‘Left’ and ‘Right’, which actually refer to the banks of the Rhône River. The left category features bigger wines with fuller and fruitier flavors. The Southern boasts a wealth of appellations that stretch from either side of the river into the mountains and valleys. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, January 24, 2024 Tudor Style Architecture By Will Adams Because England had such a strong cultural influence on early America, it was inevitable that we would inherit various architectural styles as well. While walking through Piedmont it is easy to come across the prominent Tudor style and its variants, maybe one of the most lasting of our British legacy. The Tudor we see in Piedmont today is really Tudor Revival, which was an early 1900’s reinvention of the medieval prototypes from the English Tudor dynasty of the 16th century. The Tudor style is characterized by steeply pitched, front facing gable roofs. There are, however, frequent variations and exceptions in this “playful” style of architecture with hipped roofs sometimes used in conjunction with the gables. What we end up with is a stately looking architecture that is also picturesque – the feeling of a country estate, which seems to be aesthetically suited for the large single family lots we have here. The popularity of this style in the early 1900’s was to a large degree an alternative to the modernism that was being developed in Europe with machined components and lack of ornamentation. People wanted a more handcrafted feeling that ended up being expressed in Tudor homes. As a matter of fact, the Tudor style was closely associated with the Arts and Crafts movement which was being developed at the same time for many of the same reasons. I often wonder why a certain architectural style becomes popular and then remains so for so many years. I think that certainly one reason is because these styles were well developed over a long period of time. Proportions, material selections, and detailing conventions were worked out over the years on different buildings until they became….fine architecture! Certainly. this was the case on the cathedrals that took hundreds of years to build. After building a part of it, seeing it for a few years or even decades, the sponsors and architects were able to re-design and correct functional and aesthetic components, sometimes even changing the architectural style completely. In any case, the Tudor style developed into an appealing and See Walking Piedmont on page 32 The “half-timbered” facade along with the steeply pitched gable roofs on typically two-and three-story buildings make the Tudor style easy to recognize. Intricate lower-level brick or stonework is also a common component as seen in these fine Piedmont homes. Not all Tudor homes are large manors. Tudor cottages with many of the signature hallmarks are also built. As discussed previously, this variation in building scale adds immensely to the vibrant texture and aesthetic vitality of the city of Piedmont. Artful, informal, even whimsical detailing is often found in the Tudor style. Chimneys and beautifully proportioned dormers both play a big part in the picturesque results.

The visual giveaway of course is the half-timbered walls, consisting of a squared heavy timber frame structural system originally infilled with masonry or a stucco like mixture know as wattle between the timbers. The timber frame became unnecessary a long time ago, but the look was so favored and enduring that it continues to be imitated as a decorative motif instead of a structural necessity. Another attractive characteristic of the Tudor is the sophisticated window compositions, often very vertical and large, but made up of small divided lites (panes) which were all that were available until the early 20th century. The intricate detail and sense of scale resulted in an attractive character that is popular still today, as anyone who has glanced at a Marvin or Pella window catalogue can attest. City Hall Bushy Dell comes to life Photo by Paul Hertelendy For much of the year Bushy Dell Creek, the waterway the runs through Piedmont Park, has a modest flow of water. But come December and January during the city’s rainy season, the creek comes alive with waterfalls that flow down the hillside from the Community Hall to Witter Field. A recent post-storm photo of the upper portion of Bushy Dell was taken by longtime Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy, who commented, “It hasn’t run this wild and noisy in exactly one year.” Walking Piedmont Continued from page 24 desirable architecture all over this country. The visual giveaway of course is the half-timbered walls, consisting of a squared heavy timber frame structural system originally infilled with masonry or a stucco like mixture know as wattle between the timbers. The timber frame became unnecessary a long time ago, but the look was so favored and enduring that it continues to be imitated as a decorative motif instead of a structural necessity. Another attractive characteristic of the Tudor is the sophisticated window compositions, often very vertical and large, but made up of small divided lites (panes) which were all that were available until the early 20th century. The intricate detail and sense of scale resulted in an attractive character that is popular still today, as anyone who has glanced at a Marvin or Pella window catalogue can attest. Piedmont Real Estate Update January 2024 Happy New Year! As we welcome 2024, we hope everyone enjoyed the holidays and found time to relax with family and friends. Our newsletter series began one year ago, and we greatly appreciate the positive feedback we’ve received. Each month, we aim to discuss a topic that’s timely and relevant to our readers. Research and analysis are at the core of our business; we firmly believe leveraging data creates value for our clients as they navigate the dynamic Bay Area real estate market. If there is ever something you’d like to know more about, we’d love to hear from you! It may be information that other readers would find helpful and warrant a deeper look. As we close the books on 2023, we thought it would be worthwhile to look back at median prices over the last three years in Piedmont, Berkeley, and Oakland. An unprecedented rise in interest rates began in March 2022 and had notable repercussions on the local housing market. Both the number of home sales and the median prices of homes sold were impacted. Rates are expected to come down in 2024 if inflation continues to lower and hits the Fed’s 2% target. If we don’t see an improvement in inflation, or if it rises again, we may see more rate hikes. We’ll keep a close eye on the market and always welcome a discussion about buying or selling strategies. In Piedmont, the number of home sales in 2023 was down 32% from 2021. However, the median home price was only down 5% during that same period. This speaks to the low level of available inventory but also points to the value Piedmont holds even during a slow market.
